title: Building a REAL feature with Claude Code: every step explained

synthesis.tldr: Matt Pocock guides you through implementing a real feature using Claude Code in a live production environment.
keyTakeaways: Implement a ghost course feature with a nullable filePath in the schema for ease of transition — critical for managing entities effectively.
Capture the autonomous workflow with the Ralph loop using Docker for seamless iterations and automated commit exports.
Explore TypeScript service patterns for handling ghost and real entities, ensuring real-time state transitions for effective feature deployment.
synthesis.masterSummary:
In this video, Matt Pocock takes you behind the scenes of a live coding session using Claude Code to implement a real-world feature in his extensive 1,200-commit production repository. By carefully narrating his thought process while Claude operates in the background, Matt demystifies the whole feature cycle — from brainstorming and specification to implementation and QA. Each step is rich in detail, offering developers concrete prompts and code snippets that they can directly apply to their own projects.

You'll discover how to create a 'ghost course' feature, structuring your database and service layers with TypeScript, and the impact of architectural decisions on your workflow. As you navigate through the video, be sure to check out the interactive tabs to explore code artifacts, UI designs, and even a glossary of terms that clarify the developer-AI interaction. This is more than just coding; it’s an engaging learning experience tailored for modern engineers looking to enhance their skills.

snippets.explanation: Core service layer coordinating database, file system, and path numbering logic. Each method handles state transitions for ghost/real entities. Materialize methods convert ghost entities to disk-backed real entities.
Ghost courses have null filePath; real courses have a path. This single schema change enables the ghost course feature. Courses remain real forever once a filePath is assigned.

snippets.code:
## Terms

### Ghost Entity
A database entity with no on-disk representation. Ghost lessons, ghost sections, ghost courses.

### Real Entity
An entity that exists both in the database and on the file system.

### Materialize
The act of transitioning a ghost entity to a real entity by creating its on-disk representation.
Aliases: realize, create on disk.

### Materialization Cascade
The chain reaction when materializing a lesson inside a ghost course:
1. Assign file path to course
2. Materialize section
3. Materialize lesson
snippets.explanation: Shared language document used by developer and AI agent. Prevents ambiguity when discussing feature development. Updated after each grilling session.

snippets.code:
# Sandcastle: Autonomous agent container
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /repo
RUN npm install -g pnpm
COPY . .
RUN pnpm install
# Mounts working directory, patches commits out as git diffs back to local repo
snippets.explanation: Container for autonomous agent (Ralph loop). Mounts repo, runs Claude Code agent, exports commits as patches to local filesystem. Allows repeated autonomous iterations with artifact export.

patterns.title: Service-layer boundary testing
patterns.explanation: Ghost/real state synchronization is the core risk. Boundary tests with both DB and file system ensure materializations don't corrupt state. Using Effect for testable units makes this much easier.

patterns.title: Nullable schema for optional relationships
patterns.explanation: Single source of truth: null filePath = ghost, non-null = real. Avoids dual state fields that can diverge. Simpler schema, simpler validation, simpler AI agent reasoning.

patterns.title: Ubiquitous language for AI–human communication
patterns.doExample:
// Developer: "Materialize a lesson in a ghost course"
// AI understands: trigger materialization cascade (course → section → lesson)
patterns.dontExample:
// Developer: "Make it so the thing exists on the disk"
// AI: Unclear. Create directory? Add file? Update metadata?
patterns.explanation: Shared glossary prevents AI from inventing synonyms or misunderstanding intent. When speaker and AI agree on terms (e.g., 'materialize', 'ghost entity'), reasoning becomes precise. Document in repo, reference in every session.

cheatSheet.description: Runs autonomous feature implementation while you think or QA. Check back after 1-2 hours for completed work.

cheatSheet.title: Grill Me skill (brainstorm + explore)

cheatSheet.description: Start every feature here. Lets AI challenge assumptions, spot edge cases, and read code once. More thinking upfront = less rework during implementation.

cheatSheet.title: Write PRD skill (turn grill output into structured spec)

Input: Grill Me conversation
Output: GitHub issue with user stories, acceptance criteria, module changes, testing decisions
cheatSheet.description: Converts conversational spec into actionable implementation guide. PRD becomes context for autonomous agent.

keyPoints.title: Architecture-first thinking multiplies AI effectiveness
keyPoints.detail: Before asking Claude to code, spend 20–30 minutes grilling on requirements, edge cases, and schema changes. This 'day shift' of human thinking lets the autonomous 'night shift' (Claude) run cleanly for 1–2 hours with zero interruption. Matt spent 22 minutes grilling, which compressed into a 6-issue breakdown the autonomous agent executed in 5 iterations.

keyPoints.title: Ubiquitous language (shared glossary) prevents AI misinterpretation
keyPoints.detail: When you and Claude agree on terms—e.g., 'materialize' (ghost→real transition), 'materialization cascade' (course→section→lesson chain)—every subsequent prompt is 10× clearer. Matt maintains this in a markdown file in the repo, updated after each grilling session. AI reads it automatically, avoiding invented synonyms.

keyPoints.title: Nullable schema (not boolean flags) is the single source of truth
keyPoints.detail: For ghost courses, filePath became nullable instead of adding `isGhost` boolean. Once assigned, filePath never reverts to null. This prevents state inconsistency (e.g., 'isGhost=true but filePath is set'). One field, one truth, simpler AI reasoning.

keyPoints.title: Let the AI drive clarification; ask 'trade-off' questions, not implementation questions
keyPoints.detail: When Matt wasn't sure whether to create real lessons in ghost courses immediately or always create ghosts first, he asked the AI to 'lay out the trade-offs of both approaches.' The AI showed Option A (always ghost, explicit materialize) vs. Option B (immediate materialize). Matt chose A. This forces the AI to reason, not guess.

keyPoints.title: Break PRDs into sized issues, not granular tasks
keyPoints.detail: After grill + PRD, break into 4–6 issues, each touching multiple layers (schema, service, API, UI). Too small (e.g., 'hide one UI button') = wasted agent startup cost. Too large = harder to review. Matt merged two tiny issues; ended with 4 solid slices.

keyPoints.title: Autonomous agents work best with explicit testing decisions in the spec
keyPoints.detail: The PRD included 'what to test' because it makes AI more likely to follow TDD and create feedback loops while coding. Service-layer tests (DB + file system sync) were prioritized; this guidance prevented shallow unit tests.

keyPoints.title: The 'day shift / night shift' model: humans think, AI codes in parallel
keyPoints.detail: While Claude runs autonomously in a Docker container (Ralph loop) for 1–2 hours, the developer can open a new session and grill on the *next* feature. This parallelism is revolutionary because implementation time doesn't block ideation. Matt was ready to start fresh brainstorming before QA even began.

keyPoints.title: Grill Me + Explore phase is token-efficient: sub-agent reads code, parent agent gets summary
QA plan generated from commits, not from memory
keyPoints.detail: After autonomous agent finishes, request 'Take the last 5 commits, create a step-by-step QA plan, save as GitHub issue.' The AI reads the actual code it wrote and generates testable acceptance criteria. This is more reliable than hand-written QA scripts.

keyPoints.title: QA as Feedback Loop — Issues Found in Real Usage Feed Back to Claude
keyPoints.detail: Matt uses a feedback button in the UI to capture UX issues directly. Each feedback submission auto-generates a GitHub issue with the route, description, and (via Claude) a generated title. This becomes the input for the next Ralph (autonomous agent) loop. Seven issues were discovered in ~8 minutes of QA — bugs and features missed in the brainstorm phase.

keyPoints.title: Specs-to-Code Never Captures Edge Cases — QA Iteration Finds Them
keyPoints.detail: Matt explicitly argues: 'The specs to code approach is just never going to work.' Example: if the course repo isn't a Git repository, the system enters a 'super weird state' — the directory is created in the file system but the database transaction fails, leaving them out of sync. These edge cases only surface during QA iteration, not planning.

keyPoints.title: Ralph Runs Tests and Types on Every Commit — Ensuring Quality in Autonomous Mode
keyPoints.detail: As Ralph (the autonomous agent) iterates through issues, it runs full test and type checks on each commit. Matt observes Ralph adding tests to cover new reducer actions, committing after tests pass, and closing issues. This automation ensures no regressions slip through.

keyPoints.title: Human-in-the-Loop Label Prevents Unnecessary Agent Work
keyPoints.detail: Matt adds a 'human in the loop' comment to the QA plan. The Ralph loop's prompt includes a condition: 'if there's a human in the loop like label on it or it looks like it's for humans, don't work on it.' This prevents the agent from wasting cycles on tasks that need human judgment.

keyPoints.title: Parallelizing QA and Agent Fixes — Gaps Are Features, Not Waste
keyPoints.detail: While Ralph runs in the background, Matt continues QA on other parts of the feature. He notes: 'it's quite nice having these gaps because it means that I get to do some deep focus on something... and then later I can come back.' This interleaving prevents bottlenecks and keeps momentum high.

keyPoints.title: Code Review Focuses on Inputs/Outputs, Not Line-by-Line Inspection
keyPoints.detail: Matt reflects: 'What I'm doing here is reviewing inputs and outputs... I'm interested in how the interfaces are changing, how the modules are looking. Every so often I'll go and have a little poke around in the code just to make sure it's on the right track.' He explicitly avoids deep code dives — instead, he validates behavior and passes corrected context back to Claude.

concepts.name: Ghost Entity
concepts.definition: A database entity with no on-disk file system representation. Ghost lessons, sections, and courses exist only in the database. They are a planning mechanism—you can create and organize them before committing to disk.
concepts.example: A ghost course has a name and DB row but null filePath. When you add a real lesson to it, the course materializes: gains a filePath, gets a Git repo directory, and all nested entities become real.
concepts.analogy: Like sketching an outline before writing a full document. It's a draft that you can delete, reorganize, or promote to 'real' status.

concepts.name: Real Entity
concepts.definition: An entity that exists in both the database and the file system. Once a course is real (has a filePath), it remains real forever—you can't downgrade it back to ghost.
concepts.example: A real lesson has a DB row, a directory on disk, and a file path. Deleting a real lesson purges both the DB entry and the on-disk files.

concepts.name: Materialize
concepts.definition: The action of converting a ghost entity to a real entity by creating its on-disk representation and assigning a file path. Aliases: realize, create on disk.
concepts.example: When you click 'Create Real Lesson' in a ghost course, a modal appears asking for the course file path. You provide it, and the entire chain materializes: course gets a path, section gets a directory, lesson gets files.
concepts.analogy: Like committing a draft to publication. Once published, you can edit but never unpublish.

concepts.name: Materialization Cascade
concepts.definition: The chain reaction triggered when materializing a lesson inside a ghost course. It automatically materializes the parent section and parent course in sequence, assigning a file path to the course.
concepts.example: User creates a real lesson in ghost course 'New Fun Course'. Cascade: (1) assign filePath to course, (2) create section directory, (3) create lesson files. All in one flow.
concepts.analogy: Like dominoes falling. One action triggers the rest.

concepts.name: Ubiquitous Language
concepts.definition: A shared glossary of domain-specific terms maintained in the codebase and understood by both developer and AI agent. Prevents ambiguity and invention of synonyms.
concepts.example: Instead of developer saying 'make it exist on disk' and AI guessing, both agree on 'materialize.' File stores definitions, aliases, and related concepts (e.g., 'materialization cascade').
concepts.analogy: A translator's dictionary. Without it, communication breaks down.

concepts.name: Grill Me Skill
concepts.definition: A multi-turn AI conversation that challenges assumptions, asks trade-off questions, and refines rough requirements into a precise specification. Includes an Explore phase where a sub-agent reads the codebase.
concepts.example: Matt dictated: 'Annoying to create ghost lesson then materialize it.' Grill Me replied: 'Is the pain about ceremony, or about two-step process?' and suggested alternatives. 22 minutes of back-and-forth produced an 8-item feature spec.
concepts.analogy: Like a Socratic method. The AI plays the role of Willow Reagan (Matt's mentor) asking clarifying questions.

concepts.name: Architecture-first Thinking
concepts.definition: Designing the schema, service layer, and API routes *before* asking Claude to code. This means thinking about data flow, state consistency, and testability upfront.
concepts.example: Instead of 'add real lesson creation,' Matt first asked: 'Should filePath be nullable or a separate boolean flag?' Decided on nullable, which simplified everything downstream. This decision, made during grill, saved hours of refactoring.
concepts.analogy: Building blueprints before construction. Bad architecture wastes more time than bad implementation.

concepts.name: Service Layer
concepts.definition: A testable module that encapsulates business logic for state transitions (e.g., courseRightService). It coordinates between the database, file system, and path numbering logic. Has a clear public interface.
concepts.example: courseRightService.materializeCourseAndLesson(courseId, filePath, lessonId) handles the entire cascade in one method. Tests create a test DB and temp Git repo to verify both layers sync correctly.
concepts.analogy: Like a machine's transmission. Input request → state transition → output (DB + file system).

concepts.name: Autonomous Agent (Ralph Loop)
concepts.definition: Claude Code running in a loop, pulling open GitHub issues from a repo, implementing each one, and closing issues as commits are made. Runs in a Docker container to isolate the environment. Requires well-written specs (PRDs) to succeed.
concepts.example: Matt ran `pnpm ralph`. Claude's agent fetched 6 GitHub issues, executed 5 iterations (one per issue, roughly), and generated 6 commits with detailed messages. Took ~1.5 hours, zero interruption needed.
concepts.analogy: A junior developer working through a task list overnight while you sleep. By morning, the work is done (and needs QA).

concepts.name: Day Shift / Night Shift Model
concepts.definition: The developer (day shift) spends 20–30 min grilling/designing, then the AI (night shift) runs autonomously for 1–2 hours while the developer brainstorms the next feature or steps away. This parallelism eliminates idle time.
concepts.example: Matt finished grilling at 22 minutes, issued the PRD, broke it into 6 issues, and kicked off Ralph loop. While Claude worked for 1.5 hours, Matt could have opened a new Grill Me session for a different feature. By the time QA began, the next idea was already spec'd.
concepts.analogy: A factory with two shifts: human designs, AI manufactures. No one waits.

concepts.name: QA Plan
concepts.definition: A step-by-step testing guide auto-generated from the implemented commits. Lists every user-facing change and the steps to test it, saved as a GitHub issue.
concepts.example: After 6 commits, Matt asked Claude: 'Create a QA plan for these commits.' Claude listed: (1) Create ghost course, verify no publish button, (2) Create real lesson in ghost course, verify modal appears, etc. Each step had expected outcomes.
concepts.analogy: A checklist you'd hand to a QA engineer, but auto-generated from code.

concepts.name: Ralph Loop
concepts.definition: Matt's term for a continuous autonomous agent cycle: run the agent on a batch of GitHub issues, let it fix bugs and implement features in the background while the human does other work (QA, brainstorm), then collect the results and queue up the next batch.
concepts.example: After Matt creates 7 QA issues, he runs 'pnpm ralph' and the agent autonomously fixes them while he continues testing other features. By the time he finishes QA, Ralph has closed most issues and is on iteration 8.

concepts.name: Feedback Button as QA Tool
concepts.definition: A UI component that allows Matt to describe a bug or UX issue in natural language. The system auto-generates a GitHub issue title (using Claude), includes the current route, and queues it for the Ralph loop.
concepts.example: Matt sees that creating a ghost course doesn't navigate to the new page and shows a minified React error. He clicks the feedback button, dictates the issue, and a GitHub issue is automatically created with title 'Ghost Course Creation Does Not Redirect'.

concepts.name: QA as Feedback
concepts.definition: The final phase of the feature cycle: systematically test the feature, capture issues (bugs and missed features) via the feedback button, and feed them back as GitHub issues for the Ralph loop to resolve.
concepts.example: Matt walks through the QA plan, testing the mirror course feature. Over 8 minutes, he discovers: (1) ghost course terminology in UI, (2) no navigation after creation, (3) confusing 'ghost lesson' / 'real lesson' language, (4) missing delete confirmation modal, (5) sync failure if repo is not a Git repository.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop Task
concepts.definition: A task marked in the issue or QA plan that requires human judgment and should not be worked on by the autonomous agent. The agent checks for this label and skips the task.
concepts.example: Matt adds a comment 'Ralph loops should not work on this one. This is a human in the loop task only.' The Ralph loop's prompt includes: 'if there's a human in the loop like label on it... don't work on it.'

concepts.name: Autonomous Mode (AFK Running)
concepts.definition: Setting the agent to run continuously in the background on a batch of issues while the human does other work. No interruptions, no real-time interaction — the agent executes, commits, closes issues, and reports results when done.
concepts.example: Matt says 'I'm going to start my Ralph loop as I'm going here' and immediately returns to QA without watching the agent run. 30 minutes later, he returns to find iteration 8 nearly complete with 14 commits and most issues closed.

concepts.name: Edge Case Discovery in QA
concepts.definition: The realization that thorough specifications cannot predict all edge cases — they only surface during actual QA iteration and real-world usage. Matt argues this invalidates the 'specs-to-code' approach.
concepts.example: Matt and the brainstorm team never considered: 'If the course repo is not a Git repository and anything fails, the directory is created on the file system but the database transaction rolls back, leaving them out of sync.' This was only discovered during QA.

takeaways: Spend 20–30 minutes grilling (asking clarifying questions, exploring edge cases) before writing a single line of code. This unblocks autonomous agent work for hours.
Use a ubiquitous language file (markdown) to define domain terms. Update it after each grill session. This prevents AI reinvention and keeps reasoning precise.

Design the schema and service interface before implementing. A nullable filePath (not a boolean flag) prevents state inconsistency. Good architecture costs zero lines of code, saves hours of debugging.
Break PRDs into 4–6 medium-sized issues, each touching multiple layers (schema, service, API, UI). Avoid granular tasks—they waste agent startup time.
Pair architecture decisions with explicit testing decisions in the PRD. This makes autonomous agents more likely to follow TDD and create testable units.
Use the day shift / night shift model: humans think, AI codes in parallel. While Claude runs autonomously, brainstorm the next feature. Zero idle time.
Generate QA plans from actual commits, not memory. Have the AI read what it built and create testable steps. This catches edge cases you'd miss manually.
Treat Claude Code like a senior engineer you delegate to: give it clear requirements, good architecture, feedback loops, and autonomy. Don't over-specify implementation details.
🎯 Run the agent on batches of GitHub issues in the background (Ralph loops) while you do deep QA in parallel — don't wait for each fix to complete.
💬 Use a feedback button in your UI to capture QA issues in natural language — auto-generate GitHub issues to feed back to the agent.
⏭️ Label human-in-the-loop tasks so the agent skips them and doesn't waste cycles on judgment calls.
🐛 Expect to find edge cases in QA that no spec phase could predict — plan for multiple QA → fix → QA cycles.
🔍 Review inputs/outputs and interfaces during code review, not line-by-line code — let the agent handle implementation details and you focus on behavior validation.
⚙️ Ensure the autonomous agent runs tests and types on every commit — no quality regressions slip through.
🔄 Close completed QA plans to remove them from the agent's context — prevents the agent from treating closed issues as the source of truth for new work.

learning.keyQuestion: How do you run a complete Claude Code feature cycle—from brainstorm to implemented and tested code—while maintaining tight human control over architecture and design?
learning.summary: Matt demonstrates a revolutionary workflow: spend 20–30 minutes in a 'Grill Me' session with Claude to refine vague requirements into a precise spec (with ubiquitous language), then break that spec into 4–6 medium-sized GitHub issues. A 'Ralph loop' (autonomous agent in Docker) executes all issues in 1–2 hours while you design the next feature (day/night shift parallelism). Finally, generate a QA plan from the actual commits and verify it locally. This architecture-first, specification-driven approach lets Claude Code run autonomously with minimal errors, because the spec is so clear that the AI reasons correctly about edge cases and state consistency.

synthesis.masterSummary:
In this video, Matt Pocock takes you behind the scenes of a live coding session using Claude Code to implement a real-world feature in his extensive 1,200-commit production repository. By carefully narrating his thought process while Claude operates in the background, Matt demystifies the whole feature cycle — from brainstorming and specification to implementation and QA. snippets.code:
## Terms

### Ghost Entity
A database entity with no on-disk representation. Ghost lessons, ghost sections, ghost courses.

### Real Entity
An entity that exists both in the database and on the file system.

### Materialize
The act of transitioning a ghost entity to a real entity by creating its on-disk representation.
Aliases: realize, create on disk.

### Materialization Cascade
The chain reaction when materializing a lesson inside a ghost course:
1. Assign file path to course
2. Materialize section
3. Materialize lesson

tabs.label: 6 Mental Models

concepts.name: Ghost Entity
concepts.definition: A database entity with no on-disk file system representation. Ghost lessons, sections, and courses exist only in the database. They are a planning mechanism—you can create and organize them before committing to disk.
concepts.example: A ghost course has a name and DB row but null filePath. When you add a real lesson to it, the course materializes: gains a filePath, gets a Git repo directory, and all nested entities become real.
concepts.analogy: Like sketching an outline before writing a full document. It's a draft that you can delete, reorganize, or promote to 'real' status.

concepts.name: Real Entity
concepts.definition: An entity that exists in both the database and the file system. Once a course is real (has a filePath), it remains real forever—you can't downgrade it back to ghost.
concepts.example: A real lesson has a DB row, a directory on disk, and a file path. Deleting a real lesson purges both the DB entry and the on-disk files.

concepts.name: Materialize
concepts.definition: The action of converting a ghost entity to a real entity by creating its on-disk representation and assigning a file path. Aliases: realize, create on disk.
concepts.example: When you click 'Create Real Lesson' in a ghost course, a modal appears asking for the course file path. You provide it, and the entire chain materializes: course gets a path, section gets a directory, lesson gets files.
concepts.analogy: Like committing a draft to publication. Once published, you can edit but never unpublish.

concepts.name: Materialization Cascade
concepts.definition: The chain reaction triggered when materializing a lesson inside a ghost course. It automatically materializes the parent section and parent course in sequence, assigning a file path to the course.
concepts.example: User creates a real lesson in ghost course 'New Fun Course'. Cascade: (1) assign filePath to course, (2) create section directory, (3) create lesson files. All in one flow.
concepts.analogy: Like dominoes falling. One action triggers the rest.

concepts.name: Ubiquitous Language
concepts.definition: A shared glossary of domain-specific terms maintained in the codebase and understood by both developer and AI agent. Prevents ambiguity and invention of synonyms.
concepts.example: Instead of developer saying 'make it exist on disk' and AI guessing, both agree on 'materialize.' File stores definitions, aliases, and related concepts (e.g., 'materialization cascade').
concepts.analogy: A translator's dictionary. Without it, communication breaks down.

concepts.name: Grill Me Skill
concepts.definition: A multi-turn AI conversation that challenges assumptions, asks trade-off questions, and refines rough requirements into a precise specification. Includes an Explore phase where a sub-agent reads the codebase.
concepts.example: Matt dictated: 'Annoying to create ghost lesson then materialize it.' Grill Me replied: 'Is the pain about ceremony, or about two-step process?' and suggested alternatives. 22 minutes of back-and-forth produced an 8-item feature spec.
concepts.analogy: Like a Socratic method. The AI plays the role of Willow Reagan (Matt's mentor) asking clarifying questions.

concepts.name: Architecture-first Thinking
concepts.definition: Designing the schema, service layer, and API routes *before* asking Claude to code. This means thinking about data flow, state consistency, and testability upfront.
concepts.example: Instead of 'add real lesson creation,' Matt first asked: 'Should filePath be nullable or a separate boolean flag?' Decided on nullable, which simplified everything downstream. This decision, made during grill, saved hours of refactoring.
concepts.analogy: Building blueprints before construction. Bad architecture wastes more time than bad implementation.

concepts.name: Service Layer
concepts.definition: A testable module that encapsulates business logic for state transitions (e.g., courseRightService). It coordinates between the database, file system, and path numbering logic. Has a clear public interface.
concepts.example: courseRightService.materializeCourseAndLesson(courseId, filePath, lessonId) handles the entire cascade in one method. Tests create a test DB and temp Git repo to verify both layers sync correctly.
concepts.analogy: Like a machine's transmission. Input request → state transition → output (DB + file system).

concepts.name: Autonomous Agent (Ralph Loop)
concepts.definition: Claude Code running in a loop, pulling open GitHub issues from a repo, implementing each one, and closing issues as commits are made. Runs in a Docker container to isolate the environment. Requires well-written specs (PRDs) to succeed.
concepts.example: Matt ran `pnpm ralph`. Claude's agent fetched 6 GitHub issues, executed 5 iterations (one per issue, roughly), and generated 6 commits with detailed messages. Took ~1.5 hours, zero interruption needed.
concepts.analogy: A junior developer working through a task list overnight while you sleep. By morning, the work is done (and needs QA).

concepts.name: Day Shift / Night Shift Model
concepts.definition: The developer (day shift) spends 20–30 min grilling/designing, then the AI (night shift) runs autonomously for 1–2 hours while the developer brainstorms the next feature or steps away. This parallelism eliminates idle time.
concepts.example: Matt finished grilling at 22 minutes, issued the PRD, broke it into 6 issues, and kicked off Ralph loop. While Claude worked for 1.5 hours, Matt could have opened a new Grill Me session for a different feature. By the time QA began, the next idea was already spec'd.
concepts.analogy: A factory with two shifts: human designs, AI manufactures. No one waits.

concepts.name: QA Plan
concepts.definition: A step-by-step testing guide auto-generated from the implemented commits. Lists every user-facing change and the steps to test it, saved as a GitHub issue.
concepts.example: After 6 commits, Matt asked Claude: 'Create a QA plan for these commits.' Claude listed: (1) Create ghost course, verify no publish button, (2) Create real lesson in ghost course, verify modal appears, etc. Each step had expected outcomes.
concepts.analogy: A checklist you'd hand to a QA engineer, but auto-generated from code.

concepts.name: Ralph Loop
concepts.definition: Matt's term for a continuous autonomous agent cycle: run the agent on a batch of GitHub issues, let it fix bugs and implement features in the background while the human does other work (QA, brainstorm), then collect the results and queue up the next batch.
concepts.example: After Matt creates 7 QA issues, he runs 'pnpm ralph' and the agent autonomously fixes them while he continues testing other features. By the time he finishes QA, Ralph has closed most issues and is on iteration 8.

concepts.name: Feedback Button as QA Tool
concepts.definition: A UI component that allows Matt to describe a bug or UX issue in natural language. The system auto-generates a GitHub issue title (using Claude), includes the current route, and queues it for the Ralph loop.
concepts.example: Matt sees that creating a ghost course doesn't navigate to the new page and shows a minified React error. He clicks the feedback button, dictates the issue, and a GitHub issue is automatically created with title 'Ghost Course Creation Does Not Redirect'.

concepts.name: QA as Feedback
concepts.definition: The final phase of the feature cycle: systematically test the feature, capture issues (bugs and missed features) via the feedback button, and feed them back as GitHub issues for the Ralph loop to resolve.
concepts.example: Matt walks through the QA plan, testing the mirror course feature. Over 8 minutes, he discovers: (1) ghost course terminology in UI, (2) no navigation after creation, (3) confusing 'ghost lesson' / 'real lesson' language, (4) missing delete confirmation modal, (5) sync failure if repo is not a Git repository.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop Task
concepts.definition: A task marked in the issue or QA plan that requires human judgment and should not be worked on by the autonomous agent. The agent checks for this label and skips the task.
concepts.example: Matt adds a comment 'Ralph loops should not work on this one. This is a human in the loop task only.' The Ralph loop's prompt includes: 'if there's a human in the loop like label on it... don't work on it.'

concepts.name: Autonomous Mode (AFK Running)
concepts.definition: Setting the agent to run continuously in the background on a batch of issues while the human does other work. No interruptions, no real-time interaction — the agent executes, commits, closes issues, and reports results when done.
concepts.example: Matt says 'I'm going to start my Ralph loop as I'm going here' and immediately returns to QA without watching the agent run. 30 minutes later, he returns to find iteration 8 nearly complete with 14 commits and most issues closed.

concepts.name: Edge Case Discovery in QA
concepts.definition: The realization that thorough specifications cannot predict all edge cases — they only surface during actual QA iteration and real-world usage. Matt argues this invalidates the 'specs-to-code' approach.
concepts.example: Matt and the brainstorm team never considered: 'If the course repo is not a Git repository and anything fails, the directory is created on the file system but the database transaction rolls back, leaving them out of sync.' This was only discovered during QA.

questions.question: Why does Matt make the 'filePath' nullable in the schema?
options: To allow for ghost courses that do not yet have an on-disk representation
To prevent data loss when a course is deleted
To enforce a strict validation on course names
To handle cases where file paths are unknown
questions.explanation: Making 'filePath' nullable allows ghost courses to exist without a path until they're materialized, as discussed at 22:30.

options: Fetches GitHub issues and runs the Claude Code agent
questions.explanation: The 'Ralph loop' command, defined at 36:00, is responsible for fetching open issues and executing the Claude Code agent.

questions.question: What is meant by 'materialization cascade'?
options: The effect of changes propagating through a series of state transitions
The data fetching process from the API to the database
The structure of asynchronous functions in TypeScript
The installation of multiple node packages
questions.explanation: The materialization cascade refers to the process where materializing a lesson triggers a chain of transitions, discussed in the glossary at 23:00.
